Title: Physics-Informed Digital Twins in Computational Engineering: a PRISMA-ScR Review of Physics-Informed Learning, Neural Operators, Uncertainty Quantification, Real-Time Updating, and Deployment Readiness
Abstract: Physics-informed digital twins in computational engineering require more than a simulation model or a machine-learning surrogate. They connect a physical asset to a computational representation, learn from data, quantify uncertainty, update under sensor information, and support engineering decisions under explicit latency and credibility constraints. This scoping review synthesizes six research questions on physics-informed learning, neural operators, uncertainty quantification, data assimilation, application-domain maturity, and evidence-informed method selection. Seventy-nine database-identified scholarly reports inform the synthesis; the RQ-specific counts are 15, 14, 13, 26, 27, and 17, with overlap permitted across questions. Each headline claim is appraised through test-set construction, baseline adequacy, in- versus out-of-distribution evaluation, uncertainty and failure analysis, validation provenance, and complete sensing-to-decision latency. Numerical errors, speedups, and update times are interpreted within their study-specific evaluation settings rather than as universal selection thresholds. The evidence indicates that physics-informed neural networks can support bounded inverse, surrogate, and sparse-data tasks, but their maturity is constrained by optimization pathologies, boundary enforcement, numerical baselines, and distribution shift. Neural operators provide moderate evidence of acceleration for repeated partial differential equation prediction, but only limited evidence as complete digital-twin backbones because offline cost, geometry and regime transfer, uncertainty calibration, and operational synchronization are inconsistently reported. Uncertainty quantification and data assimilation are essential credibility and synchronization layers, yet calibration non-identifiability, misuse of information-based covariance bounds, ensemble miscalibration, filter divergence, observability limits, and incomplete end-to-end validation remain common. A non-compensatory evidence-gate procedure converts the critical synthesis into method-selection guidance while preserving negative, conflicting, and unreported evidence. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework for methanol fuel supply system based on dynamic Bayesian network
Authors: Liu S.; Hu J.; Xin D.; Liu H.; Huang W.; Zhao K.
Abstract: Methanol has attracted increasing attention as a potential low-carbon marine fuel. However, the safe operation of methanol fuel supply systems is challenged by coupled hydraulic, thermal, and control dynamics, together with time-varying degradation and operational uncertainty. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework based on a dynamic Bayesian network (PDH-DBN) for methanol fuel supply systems. The framework combines a conservation law-based physics-driven model, a temporal convolutional network (TCN)-based data-driven model, online Bayesian updating through particle filter, and adaptive model fusion. The physics-driven branch updates pump-related parameters online, while the data-driven branch updates correction parameters for the TCN outputs. The two branches are then fused adaptively using their current posterior residuals. The updated parameters are further used to construct pump health indices. The proposed approach was validated on a laboratory test bench under varying flow conditions and a preset pump fault. Under normal operation, the fused framework achieved RMSEs of 0.104–0.110 Hz for pump frequency, 0.022–0.031 bar for pressure, and 0.015–0.017 °C for temperature. Under the preset pump fault scenario, PDH-DBN effectively isolated primary-pump degradation. These results indicate that PDH-DBN can support accurate state estimation, adaptive fusion, uncertainty-aware health assessment, and pump-level fault isolation for methanol fuel supply systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A digital twin framework for predictive modeling of liver-on-a-chip system dynamics using limited experimental data
Authors: Cabral T.O.; Ebrahimi A.; Bagheri A.; Khorsandi D.; Dokmeci M.R.; Jucaud V.; Pourkargar D.B.
Abstract: This study presents a data-efficient digital twin framework for a liver-on-a-chip (LoC) integrated optical biosensor platform that integrates a computational microfluidics solver with a physiologically based pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PBPK-PD) model to predict doxorubicin-induced hepatotoxicity. A learning-based model discrepancy term, trained on glutathione S-transferase alpha (GST-α) release as a biomarker, corrects structural mismatches and aligns simulations with measurements. The microfluidics module computes steady, incompressible, laminar velocity fields and transient advection-diffusion-reaction of drugs and oxygen, providing spatiotemporal concentration profiles that inform the PBPK-PD compartments. A hybrid uncertainty quantification approach, combining Bayesian inference to calibrate transport and kinetic parameters from sparse data with an XGBoost discrepancy model that captures residual bias, estimates posterior predictive intervals that account for both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties. The calibrated twin reproduces time-resolved GST-α trajectories at various dose levels, with observed responses falling within the posterior intervals. For the high-dose doxorubicin condition (20 μM), the predicted GST-α concentration shows a relative deviation of about 9% for the 2D model and 5–6% for the 3D model compared to the filtered experimental measurements. The learned discrepancy extends to previously unseen drug concentrations, enabling conservative extrapolation within quantified uncertainty bounds. Overall, the framework addresses common issues of data scarcity and model-experiment mismatch in organ-on-a-chip studies, informing preclinical decision-making for drug safety and toxicity assessments. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Sequential Bayesian parameter–state estimation in dynamical systems with noisy and incomplete observations via a variational framework
Abstract: Online joint estimation of a dynamical model’s unknown parameters and states with uncertainty quantification is crucial in many applications. For example, digital twins dynamically update their knowledge of model parameters and states to support prediction and decision-making. Reliability and computational speed are vital for DTs. Online parameter–state estimation ensures computational efficiency, while uncertainty quantification is essential for making reliable predictions and decisions. In parameter-state estimation, the joint distribution of the state and model parameters conditioned on the data, termed the joint posterior , provides accurate uncertainty quantification. Because the joint posterior is generally intractable to compute, this paper presents an online variational inference framework to compute its approximation at each time step. The approximation is factorized into a marginal distribution over the model parameters and a state distribution conditioned on the parameters. This factorization enables recursive updates through a two-stage procedure: first, the parameter posterior is approximated via variational inference; second, the state distribution conditioned on the parameters is computed using Gaussian filtering based on the approximate parameter posterior. The algorithmic design is supported by a theorem establishing upper bounds on the joint posterior approximation error. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method (i) achieves performance comparable to that of the joint particle filter in low-dimensional problems, accurately inferring both unobserved states and unknown parameters in dynamical and observation models; (ii) remains robust under noisy, partial observations and model discrepancies in a chaotic Lorenz ’96 system; and (iii) scales effectively to a high-dimensional state-space system arising from the spatial discretization of a convection–diffusion equation, outperforming the joint ensemble Kalman filter in this setting. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Toward quality-assured intelligent welding processes for aerospace structures: From process monitoring to digital closed-loop manufacturing
Authors: Peng X.; Peng S.; Wang Z.; Ma G.
Abstract: Aerospace welding is moving beyond preset-parameter automation toward process-integrated quality assurance. In this setting, material response, process observability, adaptive action, and traceable evidence must operate as coordinated functions rather than as separate technologies. This review applies a reproducible structured search covering January 2000 to July 2026, supplemented by earlier landmark sources, and classifies the literature as direct aerospace demonstration, transferable non-aerospace evidence, or conceptual enabling technology. High-strength aluminum alloys, titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, thermoplastic composites, and dissimilar joints are examined alongside friction stir, high-energy-beam, hybrid, and composite welding routes. The analysis then addresses one-, two-, and three-dimensional sensing, multimodal spatiotemporal alignment, defect and performance prediction, adaptive control, and digital-twin architectures. Evidence is comparatively mature for local sensing, defect recognition, and offline optimization. By contrast, validation remains limited for out-of-distribution reliability, physics-constrained transfer across materials and processes, millisecond-scale virtual-real closure, and certification-grade links between process signatures and residual strength or fatigue life. The proposed roadmap assigns high-fidelity models to offline learning and validation, reduced-order or surrogate models to online state estimation, and uncertainty-aware decisions to auditable safety limits. This synthesis defines the conditions required for intelligent welding to progress toward deployable, quality-assured closed-loop manufacturing of aerospace structures. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of The Society of Manufacturing Engineers.

Title: On the synthesis of the measurements and structural models using statistical finite element method
Abstract: In this paper, we present a statistical finite element method (statFEM) for the synthesis of measurement data and computational models of architected metamaterials under material and model uncertainty. The proposed framework combines a probabilistic forward model with Bayesian inference to update displacement fields using sparse, noisy observations. Synthetic measurements are generated using a high-fidelity Timoshenko beam model, while inference is performed with a reduced Euler–Bernoulli model, thereby introducing controlled model discrepancy. Material uncertainty is modelled as a Gaussian random field defined over the connectivity graph of the lattice, with a covariance structure derived from a discretised stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE). This formulation yields sparse precision matrices that enable efficient Bayesian updating for large-scale lattice systems. Numerical studies on body-centred cubic (BCC) and octet lattice structures demonstrate that the proposed approach can recover accurate solution fields from limited measurements, reduce predictive uncertainty, and identify regions most affected by model mismatch and connectivity defects. Our results show that the SPDE-based statFEM framework provides a computationally tractable and statistically rigorous approach for fusing data and models of metamaterials. It offers a promising extension to uncertainty-aware digital twins of architected materials and structures. © 2026 The Author

Title: Remaining useful life aware physics-informed Bayesian digital twin for safety-constrained control in robot-integrated battery manufacturing
Authors: A. F.; Rizwan U.; Hussainy S.T.; Almakayeel N.; Asif F.B.
Abstract: Industrial robotics cells in battery manufacturing must sustain high throughput without compromising safety under distribution shift and rare failures, yet most digital twins remain data-only, deliver uncalibrated Remaining Useful Life (RUL), or lack runtime safety mechanisms for action. To address these important limitations, we develop a Physics-Informed Bayesian Digital Twin (PI-BDT) that operationalizes a robotics-integrated prognostics-to-control pipeline. Physics-informed networks encode wear/thermal dynamics for robot-impacted stations (e.g., winding cell and calendering/oven interactions) and produce survival-based RUL with decomposed aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty via Bayesian ensembles. A shift-aware calibration loop (drift detection, uncertainty inflation, conformal quantiles) preserves nominal coverage. These distributions drive a conservative-quantile safety layer that enforces an operational risk budget (chance-constraint check) and issues explainable continue/derate/abort commands through an MPC-guided Soft Actor-Critic policy, deployable at the edge with millisecond-level latency and standard shop-floor integration (PLC/MES/ROS). On 200 pilot run-to-failure trajectories plus 500 simulated edge cases, PI-BDT achieves RUL RMSE 9.9 h, MAE 8.0 h, PICP 0.93 (95% intervals) and improves unplanned downtime by 35.2%, OEE by 22.2%, and maintenance cost by 27.4% versus a threshold baseline. The novelty is an auditable, robotics-integrated twin that maps calibrated, physics-consistent RUL to safety-constrained actions robust to shift and rare events, advancing trustworthy, computer-integrated maintenance for robotized production lines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A Self-Learning Architecture for Digital Twins with Self-Protection
Authors: C. Anderson; T. G. Walmsley; P. Patros
Abstract: The digital twin paradigm is a promising enabling technology to accelerate the decarbonisation of industrial sites that use process heat. With digital representations that look-like, behave-like, and connect to a physical system, digital twins bring together critical operational and asset data into a single knowledge store. However, a high-fidelity digital twin relying on the cloud in real-time with direct influence on operations exposes the plant to cyber attacks. We propose a software architecture for a Digital Twin that adaptively generates more accurate representations of its operations to detect malicious activities and mitigate their effects. To achieve this adaptivity, our solution leverages ML, time-series forecasting, concept drift detection and control stability analysis. To evaluate our solution, we develop a simulation of a simple industrial plant consisting of one PID-controlled steam-boiler and a variety of uncertainties. Our experimental evaluation suggests that Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Control, a system identification technique, best contributes towards Self-Learning by producing verifiable models that better align the need for retraining with concept drifts.

Title: AI-Driven Soft Sensors: Applications, Validation, and Metrological Challenges
Authors: P. S. Nzakuna; M. Eyunkoel Lasaba; V. Basemenane; E. Mutelezi; V. Paciello; A. K. Lusala
Abstract: AI-assisted soft sensors (also called virtual or inferential sensors) estimate difficult-to-measure variables from readily available measurements when direct sensing is impractical due to cost, latency, intrusiveness, or reliability constraints. Recent advances in machine learning and deep learning have expanded soft sensing from classical regression-based estimators to high-capacity models capable of learning nonlinear relationships from multivariate time series and heterogeneous sensor streams. However, deploying these models as measurement functions raises challenges beyond mere point accuracy. Key metrological hurdles include uncertainty quantification, drift under changing operating conditions, sparse reference measurements, data synchronization, and lifecycle governance for model recalibration. This paper reviews the application landscape of AI-assisted soft sensors across industrial processes, manufacturing, energy systems, environmental monitoring, and biomedical sensing, and organizes existing approaches into a practical taxonomy spanning classical machine learning, deep sequence models, hybrid/grey-box methods, online adaptation, and uncertainty-aware modeling. We then synthesize the key metrological challenges that determine trustworthiness in practice: traceability, validation protocols, uncertainty reporting, robustness to distribution shift, and data integrity; and propose a concise evaluation and reporting checklist to improve comparability and reproducibility. Finally, we outline emerging directions such as self-supervised learning, conformal prediction, physics-informed hybrids, and federated learning to support reliable soft sensing across devices, sites, and time.

Title: Water-Quality Digital Twins: A Review of Architectures, State-Space Assimilation, and Alerting
Abstract: Digital twins are rapidly becoming a rigorous framework for water-quality monitoring, converting noisy pH and total dissolved solids (TDS) measurements into reliable, decision-ready signals. This review adopts a deliberately architecture-centric lens spanning edge, fog, and cloud to examine how communications (MQTT/HTTP; LPWAN/cellular), compute placement, and orchestration (containers, device shadows, CI/CD) influence accuracy, latency, resilience, and maintainability. We consolidate sensing fundamentals and error modes, then organize data assimilation around state-space modeling: Kalman variants (KF/EKF/UKF), Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, and particle filters, augmented with robust residual tests, Huber-style losses, gap imputation, and multi-sensor fusion using temperature and conductivity for pH compensation. On the decision layer, we compare standards-aligned thresholds with hysteresis and TOT logic, probabilistic exceedance based on posterior uncertainty, and change-point detectors such as CUSUM and BOCPD for abrupt events. The survey proposes a reporting checklist and a benchmarking protocol that links twin fidelity to alert quality via continuous errors (MAE/RMSE), event metrics (precision/recall/F1, detection latency, false-alarm rate), and operational SLOs (uptime, MTTA/MTTR). Case-study archetypes, including river intakes, reservoir buoys, groundwater wells, and treatment plants, are mapped to constraints in power, bandwidth, staffing, and risk tolerance, yielding context-specific design guidance. We conclude with open challenges in drift adaptation, explainability at the edge, cybersecurity, and dataset standardization, and outline a reference setup for reproducible ablations and fair, apples-to-apples comparison. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Bio360: A Multimodal Framework for Health Digital Twin Modeling and Early Physiological Drift Detection
Authors: Karnati S.; Mukherjee S.; Dasiga S.
Abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring through wearable devices and digital health applications has become increasingly prevalent; however, clinically meaningful interpretation of these signals remains limited due to fragmented data ecosystems, heterogeneous sampling characteristics, and reliance on isolated threshold-based alerts. This paper presents Bio360, a multimodal Health Digital Twin (HDT) framework designed to integrate wearable biosignals, health and fitness applications, nutrition and lifestyle inputs, and longitudinal clinical data into a unified, continuously evolving digital health representation. The framework emphasizes longitudinal analysis, personalized baseline-relative interpretation, and contextual multisignal convergence rather than isolated physiological measurements. Bio360 incorporates a four-pillar multimodal architecture supported by a harmonization and normalization pipeline capable of integrating heterogeneous physiological streams across wearable platforms with differing temporal resolutions, signal fidelity, and device-specific schemas. The system further introduces a Contextual Event Evaluator (CEE) that aggregates baseline-relative deviations, signal weighting, and trend persistence into a composite Event Confidence Score (ECS) for identifying potentially meaningful physiological drift. To strengthen predictive interpretation under uncertainty, the framework incorporates Bayesian probabilistic modeling that continuously updates confidence estimates as new physiological and contextual data become available. A representative cardiovascular monitoring scenario demonstrates how persistent convergence among elevated resting heart rate, reduced heart rate variability, altered sleep architecture, behavioral stress patterns, laboratory biomarkers, and family history may collectively indicate emerging physiological risk despite individually nominal measurements. Bio360 further extends beyond physiological modeling through the introduction of a Behavioral Digital Twin (BDT), which incorporates adherence, behavioral routines, and wellness engagement into the broader digital twin ecosystem. The proposed framework aims to support early physiological drift detection, simulation-driven predictive health modeling, and scalable longitudinal health intelligence for future preventive healthcare systems. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Robust Field-Focused Digital Twin for Real-Time Water-Quality Estimation and Alerting
Abstract: Sensors and communications should be model-driven in the digital twin that itself accurately represents control logic, so the treatment plant has accurate sanitation evaluations for assimilation decisions (and alarm notifications) even store-and-forward hours later. This work presents a high-fidelity and hardware-realistic digital twin framework to model probe physics, temperature-dependent conductance, reference-electrode drift, telemetry loss, fouling, biofilm-growth mechanism, and the maintenance cycles in order to quantify estimator and alarm performance under normal operational stressors. The twin closes a research gap by integrating a parametric state-space model with a hybrid assimilation toolchain: lightweight Kalman updates for near-real-time denoising, Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing for retrospective optimization, and robust residual screening for outlier rejection/gap filling. An alert engine uses standards-aligned thresholds, hysteresis, and time-over-threshold (TOT) rules (with continuous monitoring of residuals using Cumulative SUM [CUSUM] statistics at individual sensor nodes), as well as residual-driven CUSUM and Bayesian online change-point detection to trade off early warning versus nuisance reduction. Results for semisynthetic scenarios calibrated to reservoir, treatment plant, and wellfield conditions are presented, showing reductions of 48.6% in RMSE for pH and 42.3% for TDS; a decrease of the false alarm rate from 12.4% to 3.1%; and a mean reduction of detection delay as high as 38%. The platform consists of a reusable field-focused testbed for algorithm selection, calibration planning, operational SLO development, and operator training guidance. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Dynamic Hierarchical Posterior Evolution for Bayesian Neural Network-Based Industrial Digital Twins under Non-Stationary Conditions
Authors: Li C.; Wang L.; Xu L.; Liu Y.; Kong Y.; Song X.
Abstract: Industrial digital twins must continuously ingest online data during long-term operation and revise the virtual-to-physical mapping under non-stationary factors such as operating-condition switching, equipment degradation, and observation bias. Conventional deterministic models cannot explicitly characterize predictive uncertainty, while existing Bayesian continual-learning methods still suffer from weak historical knowledge retention, limited physical-consistency constraints, and degraded uncertainty quality under drift. To address these issues, this paper proposes Dynamic Hierarchical Posterior Evolution (DHPE) for non-stationary industrial digital twins. In the representation layer, a hierarchical Gaussian-Inv-Gamma formulation with dynamic scale adjustment is introduced to maintain uncertainty health during online updating. In the evolution layer, complex posteriors are projected into Gaussian-mixture interface posteriors, and geometric Wasserstein distance is used to jointly incorporate historical posterior inheritance and physically anchored priors, thereby enabling smooth recursion under non-Gaussian conditions while preserving long-term physical consistency. A closed-loop mechanism integrating drift monitoring, state switching, and geometric feedback is further constructed to adaptively regulate inheritance strength, anchoring stiffness, and uncertainty width. Online experiments on titanium reduction furnace temperature prediction under three representative non-stationary scenarios show that DHPE delivers more stable error trajectories, more reasonable interval coverage, and more consistent probabilistic predictions, while maintaining strong posterior recovery capability and long-term robustness. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Adaptive Weighted Physical Prior Bayesian Neural Network for Industrial Digital Twins
Authors: C. Li; Y. Kong; Y. Liu; X. Song; Y. Ma; Q. Yue
Abstract: In the task of temperature prediction for the metallurgical industry within the context of industrial digital twins, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) can effectively enhance model accuracy by incorporating physical prior information, though prior construction poses significant challenges. Drawing inspiration from Physics-Informed neural networks (PINNs), this paper centers domain knowledge as the core of “prior construction.” By transforming physical constraints into loss functions through variational inference, prior specification is converted into a constrained optimization problem. However, in multi-physics coupling modeling, the disparity in gradient magnitudes and convergence rates among constraints like energy conservation and heat transfer boundaries can lead to optimization imbalances, coupled with unstable updates of mean and variance parameters. To address this, we propose a novel framework: based on Wasserstein distance variational inference, it first employs a Hessian-based adaptive weight scheduling mechanism (Hessian-AWM) to dynamically balance multiconstraint weights. Second, it introduces a freeze-thaw training strategy to optimize mean and variance in phases, ensuring stable convergence. In titanium smelting furnace temperature prediction experiments, this framework achieves approximately 16.6% higher accuracy than the fixed-weight BNN baseline model and outperforms multiple mainstream methods. Ablation experiments further validate its effectiveness in balancing constraints and suppressing variance oscillations, providing a feasible pathway for constructing reliable priors in industrial BNNs.

Title: Explainable and Conflict-Aware Cell Sleep Control in O-RAN via Monotonic Neural Additive Models
Authors: A. A. Al-Hameed; A. S. Alhazmi; S. H. Younus; A. J. Showail; M. A. Ahmed
Abstract: AI-driven xApps for Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) energy saving achieve substantial power reductions, but they operate as opaque models. Operators cannot audit their decisions, decompose them for cross-xApp conflict negotiation, or constrain them against physically unsafe actions under distribution shift. This paper proposes the Energy-Saving Neural Additive Model (ES-NAM), an inherently interpretable architecture for a near-real-time RAN Intelligent Controller xApp that performs multi-level Advanced Sleep Mode (ASM) control. Unlike opaque models and post-hoc explainability approaches, ES-NAM decomposes each sleep decision into independent, auditable per-feature shape functions, organized into three physically grounded groups: traffic load, radio coverage, and operational history. Hard monotonicity constraints, enforced through softplus weight reparameterization, guarantee that physically unsafe actions such as deep-sleeping a heavily loaded cell cannot occur. The guarantee holds independently of the training data. A cumulative link ordinal head preserves the natural ordering of sleep levels, and group-level attribution scores enable a tunable protocol for evidence-based conflict resolution with co-deployed xApps. On a 57-cell O-RAN-compliant simulation, ES-NAM achieves comparable energy-saving performance of opaque models baselines and achieves zero monotonicity violations on out-of-distribution data. On a 10,000-scenario conflict-resolution evaluation with held-out validation and test splits, the attribution-based protocol achieves 99.5% override precision at the data-driven operating point. Cross-dataset validation confirms that these structural guarantees transfer to unseen network conditions.

Title: Learning-Based NMPC Adaptation for Autonomous Driving Using Parallelized Digital Twin
Authors: J. P. Allamaa; P. Patrinos; H. Van der Auweraer; T. D. Son
Abstract: In this work, we focus on the challenge of transferring an autonomous driving (AD) controller from simulation to reality (Sim2Real). We propose a data-efficient method for online and on-the-fly adaptation of parametrizable control architectures such that the target closed-loop performance is optimized while accounting for uncertainties such as model mismatches, changes in the environment, and task variations. The novelty of the approach resides in leveraging black-box optimization enabled by executable digital twins (xDTs) for data-driven parameter calibration through derivative-free methods to directly adapt the controller in real time (RT). The xDTs are augmented with domain randomization (DR) for robustness and allow for safe parameter exploration. The proposed method requires a minimal amount of interaction with the real world as it pushes the exploration toward the xDTs. We validate our approach through real-world experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in transferring and fine-tuning a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) with nine parameters, in under 10 min. This eliminates the need for hours-long manual tuning and lengthy machine learning training and data collection phases. Our results show that the online adapted NMPC directly compensates for the Sim2Real gap and avoids overtuning in simulation. Importantly, a 75% improvement in tracking performance is achieved, and the Sim2Real gap over the target performance is reduced from a factor of 876 to 1.033.

Title: A Risk-informed Approach to Trustworthiness Assessment in Digital Twins-based Autonomous Control
Authors: Cittadino N.; Athe P.; Lin L.; Dinh N.
Abstract: In autonomous control systems, digital twins (DTs) are used to perform diagnostic and prognostic functions. The trustworthiness of these DTs is dependent on quality and coverage of the training data, model accuracy and integrity of sensor data. This work introduces a methodology to determine the trustworthiness of a DT system given faulty sensor data using a risk informed approach. Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs) are used to propagate uncertainties and determine the probability of trustable recommendations. The decision to trust the control action provided by the DT is based on the DT output, expert opinion, and severity of problems. The performance of DTs is reliant on the data they are trained on. When they encounter out of distribution data, the trustworthiness of the recommendations decreases. To address this issue, we include an expert component that provides input on sensor degradation. For this, we utilize a generative artificial intelligence (AI) model, such as Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT). The GPT functions as an expert with broad knowledge. The GPT is fine-tuned to understand and discriminate sensor degradation scenarios using manufactured data. This methodology is demonstrated through a case study on a Nearly Autonomous Management and Control System (NAMAC) during a steady state scenario. Various sensor degradation types with different severity levels are considered. Degraded sensor data is processed by the DT system and the fine-tuned GPT. Finally, using the BBN, we combine the GPT information and the DT output with its sources of uncertainty. This provides an output regarding the trustworthiness of the DT recommendation. © 2025 AMERICAN NUCLEAR SOCIETY, INCORPORATED, WESTMONT, ILLINOIS 60559.

Title: Tool-Health Digital Twin for CNC Predictive Maintenance via Innovation-Adaptive Sensor Fusion and Uncertainty-Aware Prognostics
Authors: Cao Z.; Chen L.; Li C.; Zhu L.; Deng Z.
Abstract: A tool-health digital twin for CNC predictive maintenance is developed and operationalised as a fusion-and-state-estimation core that produces a latent tool-health trajectory (wear level and wear-rate dynamics) from multi-rate sensor streams for diagnosis and remaining useful life (RUL) forecasting under strict edge latency constraints. The scope is tool-health–informed maintenance decisions (condition-based tool replacement/scheduling), rather than a comprehensive maintenance twin for all CNC subsystems. Multi-rate vibration, spindle-current, and temperature signals are synchronized and windowed, and a linear state-space model with Kalman filtering and innovation-guided adaptive noise estimation stabilizes the latent health state across operating-regime changes. The fused state is then used by compact sequence learners, an LSTM for edge feasibility, and a compact Transformer as a higher-accuracy comparison, to output fault categories and RUL estimates. Predictive uncertainty is quantified via a Monte Carlo dropout and linked to reliability-aware actions through a simple alarm/defer/schedule policy, while SHAP provides feature-level interpretability. On a CNC testbed, fusion improves fault F1 from 0.811 to 0.892 and PR-AUC from 0.867 to 0.918 while reducing RUL RMSE from 10.4 to 8.1 cycles; the compact Transformer reaches 0.903 F1 and 7.9-cycle RMSE at higher inference time. The end-to-end pipeline remains within a ≤100 ms breakdown, maintains in-band innovation statistics, supports rehearsal-based updates under drift, and is additionally evaluated on external tool-wear and turbofan datasets. © 2026 by the authors.
